tasks.short: Take the health questions, discuss goals and limits, test the client, write and check the programme, send it to the client and review progress.

steps.what: Client answers health and goals questions at intake
Trainer goes through the health and goals questions on a paper form at intake
Trainer discusses goals, needs and physical conditions with the client
Trainer tests the client's strength, mobility and fitness
Trainer writes a suitable training program in a spreadsheet to meet special requirements
Trainer checks the final programme against the client's test results, conditions and limits, and that it is for this client
Trainer releases the checked programme to the client: printed or e-mailed today, sent once from the member app after the change
Trainer reviews progress with the client and adjusts the programme

tasks.design: Clients fill in the health and goals questionnaire online in the gym's member app ({OTHER}) before the intake, so the trainer reviews answers instead of reading out questions. The trainer builds the programme from templates and the gym's exercise library in the app, which fill in exercise descriptions; the trainer still chooses and doses every exercise, checks the final programme against the client's tests and limits, and releases it to the client. Talking, testing and progress reviews stay in person.
tasks.previous_blocker: Intake forms were paper and programmes were built in spreadsheets from scratch.
tasks.enabler_now: Gym member apps hold questionnaires, exercise libraries and programmes.
tasks.still_hard: Health answers are special-category data; templates must not replace adapting to the person.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing how a client really moves and what they are afraid of.

reach.task: Hand over clients to the gym
reach.learn: Whether shared programmes in the app ease handovers.

evidence.claim: Gym member apps hold health questionnaires, exercise libraries and programmes.
Health answers are special-category data; a tool that holds them needs a processor contract.

assumptions: Boundary: from intake to the first progress review; nutrition advice is outside.
Input contract: questionnaire filled in by the client; exercise library and templates kept by the gym manager; fallback is paper and spreadsheets.

Talking, testing, reviews and the final check keep their full time. s1 keeps 50 because the trainer still reads every answer and asks about flagged health items. s4 keeps 75 because the library fills exercise descriptions and layout, while choosing and dosing exercises stays with the trainer. s5 keeps 20 for the release itself.
Manager time is outside the trainer's savings.
Health answers are special category data under GDPR art 9: the client gives explicit consent in the app, and only the trainer and the client see them.
research_questions: Do clients stick to programmes they receive in the app?

incremental.description: No ongoing upkeep for the trainer: the gym manager keeps the library and templates, and learning the builder is a one-off.

approvals.approved_version: The programme exactly as checked by the trainer in s4c, sent once to this client's account in the member app; any change needs a new check and release.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: clients with complex conditions need programmes built mostly from scratch and many fill in the questions at intake, not before (6.7); high: clients answer online and templates fit most programmes (15.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Watch and cue intensity, explain exertion zones, check participants' heart rate and tick attendance.

steps.what: Trainer watches participants and cues them to keep exertion levels up or down
Trainer explains heart-rate zones and perceived exertion to maximize benefits from exercise routines
Participants who opt in put on and pair a heart-rate strap before class
Trainer checks participants' heart rate: by asking each one today, by reading the studio screen for strap wearers and asking the others after the change
Participants scan their member card at the studio door as the class starts
Trainer records class attendance: ticks a paper list today; after the change checks the scanned list and adds those who did not scan

tasks.design: Participants who opt in wear a heart-rate strap, and a screen in the studio shows each person's zone, so the trainer reads it at a glance instead of asking each participant during the class. Attendance is recorded when participants scan their card at the studio door in the gym's member system ({OTHER}), and the trainer adds those who did not scan; cueing and explaining stay with the trainer.
tasks.previous_blocker: Heart rates were asked out loud and attendance ticked on paper.
tasks.enabler_now: Studio heart-rate displays and check-in scans are common in gyms.
tasks.still_hard: Heart rate is health data; participants must opt in and the screen must show first names only.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing the participant who is pushing too hard before the screen does.

reach.learn: Whether check-in data show which classes fill.

evidence.claim: Studio heart-rate displays show each participant's zone from a chest strap.
Heart-rate data are health data; collect them only with explicit opt-in.

assumptions: Boundary: one class from start to attendance; class planning is outside.
Input contract: straps paired by members who opt in; check-in scanner run by the front desk; fallback is asking and paper.

Cueing and explaining keep their full time. s3 keeps 50 because only participants who opt in wear a strap; the others are still asked. s4 keeps 15 for checking the scanned list and adding participants who forgot to scan.
Heart-rate data are not stored after the class.
Participants' strap pairing (s3w) and door scans (s4m), share 1 each, are customer time outside the trainer's savings.
unknowns: Share of participants who would opt in.
research_questions: Do participants spend more time in their target zone?

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: few participants opt in to straps and many forget to scan (6.8); high: about half wear straps and most scan (11.8).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Demonstrate equipment, watch the client try it and correct form, and give machine settings in writing.

steps.what: Trainer demonstrates use of training equipment such as weights and trampolines
Trainer watches the client try the equipment and corrects form
Trainer notes the client's machine settings and personal cues: on a card today, in the client's page of the member app after the change

tasks.design: Each machine carries a code that opens a short video and the standard cues in the gym's member app ({OTHER}), and the trainer only notes the client's personal settings there. Demonstrating and correcting form stay fully with the trainer.
tasks.previous_blocker: Settings and cues were written on cards that got lost.
tasks.enabler_now: Gym apps can link machine codes to videos and personal settings.
tasks.still_hard: Videos do not see bad form; correction needs the trainer.
tasks.human_edge: Spotting the rounded back before it becomes an injury.

reach.learn: Whether machine codes cut repeat questions.

evidence.claim: Gym apps link machine codes to instruction videos and members' settings.
Teaching equipment use touches no high-risk AI area; no AI is used.

assumptions: Boundary: from demonstration to settings noted; programme design is outside.
Input contract: videos and cues per machine made by the gym manager; fallback is cards.
Demonstrating and correcting keep their full time. s3 keeps 60 because the standard cues come from each machine's page; the trainer still writes the client's settings and personal cues.
Manager time is outside the trainer's savings.
research_questions: Do members ask fewer machine questions?

incremental.description: No ongoing upkeep for the trainer: entering clients' settings is the work in s3, and the gym manager keeps the videos and cues.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: only a few machines have a page, so most cues are still written (1.0); high: every machine has its page (4.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Explain rules to new members, correct unsafe use on the floor, check signed declarations, check acceptance at entry and write incident reports.

steps.what: Trainer explains safety rules and regulations to new members
Trainer walks the floor and enforces safe use of exercise equipment
New member reads the house rules and fills in the health declaration on paper
Trainer files the paper health declaration and signed house rules
Trainer checks the paper file when unsure whether a member signed the rules
Trainer writes incident reports: on paper today, in a short form of the member system after the change
Trainer checks the final incident report: what happened, who was involved and what was done, as seen on the floor
Trainer submits the checked incident report to the gym manager

tasks.design: Members accept the house rules and fill in the health declaration online when they join the gym's member system ({OTHER}), and the check-in scan admits only members who have accepted. Incident reports use a short form in the same system where the trainer still writes what happened, checks the report and submits it to the gym manager; explaining rules and correcting unsafe use stay in person.
tasks.previous_blocker: Declarations and rules were signed on paper and filed by staff.
tasks.enabler_now: Gym member systems take online sign-ups and control check-in.
tasks.still_hard: Accepting rules online is not understanding them; safety is enforced on the floor.
tasks.human_edge: Stopping a member before a dropped weight hurts someone.

reach.learn: Whether form reports show risky equipment.

evidence.claim: Gym member systems take online sign-ups with rule acceptance and control check-in.
Health declarations are special-category data; keep them with restricted access.

assumptions: Boundary: from new member to incident reported; insurance claims are outside.
Input contract: house rules and declaration form set by the gym manager; check-in rules configured by the front desk lead; fallback is paper.

Explaining and enforcing on the floor keep their full time, and so do checking and submitting incident reports. s3 keeps 20 for following up declarations with flagged health answers. s5 keeps 85 because the form only fixes the layout; the trainer still writes the report.
Manager time is outside the trainer's savings.
Members already fill in paper forms; accepting online takes about the same time, priced as customer time.
Health declarations are special category data under GDPR art 9: members give explicit consent online, and only staff who need them can open them.
research_questions: Do incident reports become more complete with a form?

incremental.description: No ongoing upkeep: the gym manager sets the forms and check-in rules, and learning the incident form is a one-off.

approvals.approved_version: The incident report exactly as checked by the trainer in s5c, submitted once to the gym manager's queue in the member system; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: many members still join at the desk on paper, so half the filing and file checks stay (8.1); high: members join online (14.9).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The fitness trainer keeps testing, coaching and safety on the floor; paper forms, lists and cards go.
role.ambitious_version: A trainer who spends every paid minute coaching people, not filling in forms.

job.title: Exercise Trainers and Group Fitness Instructors
